newsitem.title: USA: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- Spreads widen after Fed holds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- Spreads widen after Fed holds.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury yield curve stuck perfectly to its script on Tuesday and steepened after the Federal Reserve decided to leave rates unchanged.

The curve from the two-year note to 30-year bond closed at 70 basis points -- its widest closing level since April 4 and five basis points wider than 65 basis points late Monday. Shortly after the Fed's decision, the spread had been as wide as 72 basis points (6.22 percent on the two-year note and 6.95 percent on bonds) as the shorter end cheered the Fed, while the longer end tried to figure out what to do.
"There probably is more steepness to go," said Bill Kirby, co-head trader at Prudential Securities Inc. "Maybe a nickel, perhaps more."
Gains at the short-end, though, were seen capped as long as the market expectedthe Fed to hike rates at its next policy-setting meeting in early July.

Larry Dyer, Treasury market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp, said the steepening was mostly technical in that flattening trades were taken off, since carry becomes more attractive at the short end.
"Anyone who owned bonds against two-years was supposed to take that trade off when the Fed did not move," he said. They did, so "most things are behaving as they should."
The market, however, is in better shape than when the Fed tightened policy on March 25. Yields are currently seven to 10 basis points lower than after that quarter-point rate hike.
But the two-year to 30-year spread was flatter on March 25, narrowing to 66 basis points from 68 a day earlier.

The direction of the curve going forward is expected to lie with upcoming economic data. Should economic repoerts continue to come in on the weak side, analysts predicted yields on the two-year note could fall below 6.15 percent and yields on 30-year paper could slip below 6.80 percent.

Tom Macirowski, senior Treasury strategist at Goldman, Sachs & Co Inc, said it was possible the two-year note could fall as low 6.05 percent and bonds to 6.75 percent. "The market has the potential to do better," he said. "It's conditional on the data."

Helping the front end, players said, was an abundance of cash that was sitting on the sidelines. In the wake of the Fed's leaving rates alone, that money was put to work, evidenced by bill rates falling eight to 13 basis points.

On the flip side, the continued deterioration of the dollar could weigh on the market, some noted. And, said Kirby, "The Fed still having to make another move hanging over the market's head may prevent a sustained rally."
